newsitem.title: USA: N.Carolina feed mills, meatpackers brace for storm.
newsitem.headline: N.Carolina feed mills, meatpackers brace for storm.

text.p: Many North Carolina feed mills are closing down early on Thursday as they brace for Hurricane Fran's arrival within the next 24 hours, plant managers said.

Large pork packing plants in the state would confirm no closure plans this morning but hog dealers expected that hog supplies were sure to be short due to heavy rains. "I don't know where they'll get the hogs," one Raleigh dealer said.

"We will probably be shutting down by six or seven (pm EDT)," said Rudy Hasty, manager of Nash Johnson and Son Inc, a feed mill in Rosehill, N.C. "Hopefully, if we have the power, we will be up by Friday morning.

Heavy rain and wind gusts slammed the Carolina coast on Wednesday and North Carolina governor Jim Hunt declared a state of emergency, with up to 500,000 people expected to be evacuated. The state has had 11 inches of rain in 12 hours.
"We've had tremendous flooding in the west. We've got roads washed out and this is going to come on top of that," Hunt said."
Fran, packing 115 mile-per-hour winds, was expected to hit beach communities near the North and South Carolina border late on Thursday or early Friday, the National Hurricane Center said.
At midday Thursday its center was 170 miles southeast of Myrtle Beach, S.C.
North Carolina in recent years has become the second largest hog producing state after Iowa, and it is also a large producer of feed for poultry in the Southeast.
The Nash Johnson feedmill produces 17,000 short tons per week of feed for chickens, turkeys and hogs and normally runs 24-hour shifts five to six days a week, Hasty said.
"If this storm is as severe as it makes out to be, I imagine other mills will be down," Hasty said.
Hasty stressed the temporary closure will not affect immediate supplies: "We already have feed that is produced prior to today and we are able to meet our commitments."
Jim Carr, a feed mill manager with Prestage Farms Inc in Clinton, N.C., said his company will be closing two feed mills which produce about 18,000 short tons of feed per week.

"About 10 major feed mills within a 50-mile radius of Clinton will be shutting down," Carr said. "We will probably shut down about 6:00 (PM EDT). We are hoping to start up at about 7:00 or 8:00 in the morning if we have power."

North Carolina's largest hog slaughtering plant is located in Tar Heel, about 70 miles inland from the coast and directly in the path of Fran's expected landfall. The plant's operator, Smithfield Foods, declined comment on any plans to close.
The Tar Heel plant has an estimated daily slaughter capacity of 20,000 to 24,000 head, industry sources said.

Officials of Lundy Packing, which operates a hog plant in Clinton, N.C., also declined to comment on possible closings. The plant has an estimated slaughter capacity of 8,000 hogs a day, industry sources said.
Pork industry sources in the area said the packing plants would likely not stay down long, if they did close.

"I don't know that it really would affect hog slaughter unless electricty goes off and stays off for three or four days," said Walter Cherry, executive director of the North Carolina Pork Producers Council.
